'''William Warren Bartley III''' (October 2, 1934 – February 5, 1990), known as '''W. W. Bartley III''', was an [[American philosopher]] specializing in [[20th century philosophy]], language and logic, and the [[Vienna Circle]].<ref name = "Marquis Who's Who">{{cite book |chapter=  BARTLEY, William Warren, III |title=Marquis Who's Who in the World |publisher= Macmillan Information Company |place= Wilmette, Illinois, USA |edition= 10th 1991-1992 |year = 1990 |url= https://archive.org/details/whoswhoinworld10edunse/page/n5/mode/2up |url-access= registration |page=[https://archive.org/details/whoswhoinworld10edunse/page/66/mode/2up 66] |accessdate= 23 January 2026 |via= [[Internet Archive]]}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Born in [[Wilkinsburg, Pennsylvania]], on October 2, 1934, Bartley was brought up in a Protestant home. He completed his secondary education in Pittsburgh and studied at [[Harvard University]] between 1952 and 1956, graduating with a BA degree in philosophy.<ref name="artigas">Mariano Artigas: ''The Ethical Nature of Karl Popper's Theory of Knowledge'' (1999)</ref>{{rp|18}} While an undergraduate at Harvard, he was an editor at ''[[The Harvard Crimson]]'' newspaper.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://bartleyinstitute.org/shelf/about/|title=About Bartley and the Institute|work=The Bartley Institute|access-date=24 January 2014|archive-date=February 2, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140202190308/http://bartleyinstitute.org/shelf/about/|url-status=usurped}}</ref>  He spent the winter semester of 1956 and the summer semester of 1957 at the [[Harvard Divinity School]] and the [[Episcopal Theological School]] in [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]]. In 1958, he completed his [[Master of Arts|MA]] degree in philosophy at Harvard. Bartley was training to become a Protestant minister, but rejected Christianity at that point.<ref name="artigas"/>{{rp|44f}} He went on to study under Sir [[Karl Popper]] at the [[London School of Economics]], where he completed his PhD in 1962. Parts of his dissertation, ''Limits of Rationality: A Critical Study of Some Logical Problems of Contemporary Pragmatism and Related Movements'', were subsequently published as ''The Retreat to Commitment'' in the same year.

==Career==
After his doctoral graduation, Bartley worked as a lecturer in logic in London. In the following years, he held positions at the [[Warburg Institute]] and the [[University of California, San Diego]].<ref>{{cite book |first= David |last= Miller |author-link= David Miller (philosopher)|chapter= Comprehensively Critical Rationalism: An Assessment: ''In Memory of Bill Bartley (1934-1990)'' |title= Critical Rationalism: A Restatement and Defence |publisher= Open Court |place= La Salle, Illinois |year= 1994 |url= https://archive.org/details/criticalrational0000mill/page/n5/mode/2up?view=theater |url-access=registration |pages= [https://archive.org/details/criticalrational0000mill/page/74/mode/2up?view=theater 75]- |via= [[Internet Archive]]}}</ref> He began teaching at the [[University of Pittsburgh]] in 1963, and was appointed to his first full professorship there in 1969.

In 1973, he joined the [[California State University, Hayward]] faculty as a professor of philosophy, where he received the distinction of "Outstanding Professor" of the entire [[California State University]] system in 1979. His last position there before his retirement was that of a senior research fellow at the [[Hoover Institution]].<ref name="radnitzky">Gerard Radnitzky: [http://www.law.keio.ac.jp/~popper/v2n1radnitzky2.html William W. Bartley III (1934–1990)]. ''Popper Letters'' '''2''':1 (1990)</ref>

==Relationship with Sir Karl Popper==
Bartley and Popper had a great admiration for each other, partly because of their common stand against [[justificationism]].<ref>Karl R. Popper: On the Sources of Knowledge and of Ignorance. ''Proceedings of the British Academy'' '''46''' (1960), p. 39–71, reprinted in ''Conjectures and Refutations''.</ref> However, at the International Colloquium in the Philosophy of Science at Bedford College, University of London, July 11–17, 1965, they came into conflict with each other. Bartley had presented a paper, "Theories of Demarcation Between Science and Metaphysics," in which he accused Popper of displaying a positivist attitude in his early works and proposed that Popper's demarcation criterion was not as important as Popper thought it was. Popper took this as a personal attack, and Bartley took his reply as indicating that Popper was ignoring his criticism.<ref name="artigas"/>{{rp|81f}} Their friendship was not restored until 1974, after the publication of ''The Philosophy of Karl Popper'' (edited by Paul Schillpp).<ref name="artigas"/>{{rp|87}} Bartley changed the tone of his remarks about Popper's criterion of demarcation, making it less aggressive. However, despite the restored friendship, Bartley's view was never accepted by Popper, who criticised it even after Bartley's death.<ref name="artigas"/>{{rp|First Part}}<ref>Kiichi Tachibana: [http://www.law.keio.ac.jp/~popper/v5n1tachibana.html Mails exchanged between Prof. Tachibana and Prof. Agassi On the Kyoto Prize Workshop]. ''Popper Letters'' '''5''':1 (November 17, 1992)</ref>

==Author and editor==
Bartley published a biography of the philosopher [[Ludwig Wittgenstein]], titled simply ''Wittgenstein'', in 1973.<ref>William Warren Bartley III, ''Wittgenstein'', Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1973.</ref> The book contained a relatively brief, 4–5 page treatment of Wittgenstein's homosexuality, relying mainly on reportage from the philosopher's friends and acquaintances. This matter caused enormous controversy in intellectual and philosophical circles; many perceived it as a posthumous "attack" on Wittgenstein.<ref name=Madigan>{{cite web|last=Madigan|first=Timothy J.|title=The Uses and Abuses of Philosophical Biographies|url=http://philosophynow.org/issues/35/The_Uses_and_Abuses_of_Philosophical_Biographies|work=Philosophy Now 2012|publisher=Philosophy Now|access-date=28 December 2012}}</ref> For example one review by [[Reuben Goodstein]] criticized what he called Bartley's "vicious and unsubstantiated charge of promiscuity ... written in language which is calculated to give the maximum offence both to Wittgenstein's family and to the many who knew and admired him". He adds that "Bartley's claim to have met in the parks and bars of Vienna men who remembered chance encounters with Wittgenstein more than fifty years ago is as mischievously irresponsible as his pretence to support the charge by quotations from letters which in fact do not at all support the construction Bartley places upon them".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Goodstein |first1=R.L. |title=Review: Wittgenstein By W. W. Bartley Philadelphia and New York: J. B. Lippincott Co., 1973, 192 pp. |journal=Philosophy |date=1973 |volume=48 |issue=186 |pages=403–4|doi=10.1017/S0031819100042376 }}</ref>

Some foreign translations of the book, such as the first edition of the Spanish translation, omitted the "offending" material. In the second edition of the biography (La Salle, Illinois: Open Court, 1985, pp.&nbsp;159–97), Bartley answered the objections of critics, pointing out that Wittgenstein's periods of active homosexuality are verified by the philosopher's own private writings, including his coded diaries, and that extensive confirmation was also available from people who knew Wittgenstein in Vienna between the two World Wars, including ex-lovers. Bartley also considered, and rejected, the idea of a connection between the private life and the philosophy.<ref name=Madigan />

Bartley also wrote a biography of [[Werner Erhard]], the founder of [[Erhard Seminars Training]]. Bartley was graduate of Erhard Seminars Training and served on its advisory board.<ref>{{cite book|last=Ankerberg|first=John and John Weldon|title=Encyclopedia of New Age Beliefs: The New Age Movement|year=1996|publisher=Harvest House Publishers|location=Eugene OR|isbn=978-1565071605|pages=263|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SghdYBbMds0C}}</ref>

Bartley edited [[Lewis Carroll]]'s book ''Symbolic Logic'' (see [[symbolic logic]]), including the second volume, which Carroll had never published.<ref>{{cite book|last=Gardner|first=Martin|title=The Universe in a Handkerchief: Lewis Carroll's Mathematical Recreations, Games, Puzzles, and Word Plays|year=1998|publisher=Springer|location=New York|isbn=978-0387256412|pages=61|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=77kcKHmLZXIC}}</ref>

Bartley extended Popperian epistemology in his book ''The Retreat to Commitment'',<ref name=Wettersten>{{cite encyclopedia|last=Wettersten|first=John R.|title=Karl Popper and Critical Rationalism|url=http://www.iep.utm.edu/cr-ratio/|encyclopedia=Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy|publisher=The IEP|access-date=28 December 2012}}</ref> in which he describes [[pancritical rationalism]] (PCR), a development of [[critical rationalism]] and [[panrationalism]]. PCR attempts to work around the problem of ultimate commitment or infinite regress by decoupling criticism and justification.<ref name=Rowbottom>{{cite book|last=Rowbottom|first=Darrell P.|title=Popper's Critical Rationalism: A Philosophical Investigation|year=2011|publisher=Routledge|location=New York|isbn=978-0415992442|pages=12|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e7if7wIK2koC}}</ref>  A pancritical rationalist holds all positions open to criticism, including PCR, and never resorts to authority for justification.<ref name=Rowbottom />

Parts of Popper's ''Realism and the Aim of Science'', a book that Bartley edited, and the Addendum to the fourth edition of ''The Open Society and Its Enemies'' contain passages that are commonly interpreted as Popper's acceptance of Bartley's views. [[Mariano Artigas]] held that these were in fact written by Bartley himself.<ref name="artigas"/>{{rp|23–25, 96}}

[[Alan Ebenstein]], a biographer of [[Friedrich Hayek|F. A. Hayek]], criticized Bartley for the extent of the changes he made as the editor of ''[[The Fatal Conceit]]'', a book attributed to Hayek.<ref>Alan Ebenstein: [http://libertyunbound.com/archive/2005_03/ebenstein-deceit.html Investigation: The Fatal Deceit] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080212040658/http://libertyunbound.com/archive/2005_03/ebenstein-deceit.html |date=February 12, 2008 }}. ''Liberty'' '''19''':3 (March 2005)</ref> [[Bruce Caldwell (economist)|Bruce Caldwell]] suggests that the book in its published form may actually have been written by Bartley.<ref>''Karl Popper, a Centenary Assessment Vol. 1: Life and Times, and Values in a World of Facts'', p. 120</ref>

==Death==
Bartley died of [[bladder cancer]] on February 5, 1990, at his home in Oakland, California, after having been diagnosed with the disease in the middle of the preceding year.<ref name="radnitzky"/><ref>Stephen Kresge: [http://www.law.keio.ac.jp/~popper/v2n1kresge.html On the Passing of W. W. Bartley III]. ''Popper Letters'' '''2''':1 (1990)</ref><ref name="nytobit">anonymous; [https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9C0CEED91539F931A15751C0A966958260 Obituary: "William W. Bartley 3d, Research Fellow, 55"], ''New York Times'' February 22, 1990 (corrected February 24, 1990).</ref>

At the time of his death, Bartley had just finished his last book, ''Unfathomed Knowledge, Unmeasured Wealth: On Universities and the Wealth of Nations''. Other works he was preparing at that time included writing a biography, and editing the collected works, of [[Friedrich Hayek]]. The latter was being completed after Bartley's death by his colleague and executor [[Stephen Kresge]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Caldwell|first=Bruce J.|title=Review of "Friedrich Hayek: A Biography"|url=http://www.independent.org/publications/tir/article.asp?a=165|work=The Independent Review|publisher=Independent Institute|access-date=28 December 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title= OBITUARY: Stephen Patrick Kresge (November 3, 1935 – November 12, 2018) |url= https://www.dignitymemorial.com/obituaries/pacific-grove-ca/stephen-kresge-8056811 |publisher= www.dignitymemorial.com|accessdate= 30 June 2026 }}</ref>  Also unfinished was a biography of Popper. Both biographies were in an advanced stage at the time of Bartley's death.<ref name="radnitzky"/>
